claims.text: The starting particles are sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
The starting nanoparticles are in a disordered solid-solution state.
High mixing entropy and sluggish bulk diffusion have been proposed to promote retention of an equiatomic solid solution.
The sluggish-diffusion hypothesis for high-entropy alloys is not well supported by experimental data.
For Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt particles smaller than 15 nm, surface-to-volume effects dominate over configurational-entropy stabilization.
At sub-10 nm sizes, high particle surface energy lowers the activation barrier for surface diffusion.
Enhanced surface diffusion during heating causes rapid elemental segregation.
Au and Pt are low-surface-energy elements that segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation depletes other alloying elements from the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-energy minimization overrides bulk configurational-entropy effects in these nanoparticles.
Heating drives Ostwald ripening in which smaller particles dissolve and feed larger particles.
Particles smaller than 5 nm will be rapidly lost by dissolution during annealing.
Surface segregation will produce significant shape anisotropy in the remaining particles.
Core-shell or otherwise segregated structures will form within one hour at 1000 K.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk diffusion limitations may dominate and sluggish-diffusion behavior may become valid.
The critical size at which surface effects overtake entropy stabilization is not known exactly.
Surface facets and initial defect density may alter the operative kinetic pathways.
A thin inert oxide shell will suppress surface diffusion relative to unpassivated particles.
Better retention of size and equiatomic composition in passivated particles would favor a surface-diffusion mechanism.
Identical rapid phase separation and particle loss in passivated and unpassivated samples would be interpreted as evidence for bulk-diffusion control.
